speaker_role: self-described former UC Berkeley application reader turned admissions coaching company head ('Coach Tony')
commercial_incentive: Strong: runs a paid coaching business and ends with a free-call funnel and book promotion.
key_insights: UC readers see school context first, then student data, and GPA gets only a moment because grades alone say little without course rigor and circumstances.
UCs are test blind, so domestic applicants should not submit SAT or ACT scores; AP and IB results can be reported and do not hurt.
Only a-g courses show up, ninth-grade courses are visible even though UC GPA starts in tenth, and senior-year schedules are seen.
Activities have 20 slots that UC does not rank; six categories, and self-classification has no right or wrong.
The personal insight questions are the heart of the application; readers want the 'why' behind actions, and he recommends staying near the top of the 350-word limit.

He says about 15 percent of applicants get an augmented review invitation in December, and receiving one signals a borderline first-read result; treat the optional recommendations as effectively required.
Readers are trained on 13 comprehensive review factors, bias awareness and calibration by all reading the same files; each file gets at least two reads before committee.
He advises against writing about the pandemic and says demographics are hidden from readers.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Coach Tony: 18 percent of UC slots reserved for out-of-state and international students.
Coach Tony: 13 comprehensive review factors; 8 essay prompts, choose 4, 350 words max each.
Coach Tony: about 15 percent of applicants receive augmented review, usually in December; readers begin reading in early November.
Coach Tony: UCLA (as captioned) admits by major and 55 percent of applicants apply to one of 10 majors; most UCs admit by college.
notable_or_distinctive: Offers detailed UC-specific mechanics such as augmented review, hidden demographics and the a-g visibility rules.
reliability_notes: Live webinar with sales framing, unverified statistics, heavy caption garbling, and some content that is a UC-specific process, not general admissions; the title overstates what is covered.
